replies.author: silphotographer
replies.body:
40 bucks is not a problem. People pay more than that for cheap entertainment. The bigger problem is your capital risk. If it's not huge and you are tortured by FOMO then go ahead. Maybe you win biggie. But that's gambling not investing and nothing wrong with fun gambling just know that it's not calculated bet and you should be prepared for big losses. 

You cannot stress test it unless you know the algo. Longer timespan does help but not necessarily the best way. For example, many companies went bankrupted, delisted, etc. If your AI backtest, it will ignore all those companies that failed because they are no longer on the database.  As such, you could argue that the AI cherry picked from the ones that survived thus far. It's like saying you looked at the Harvard graduates and you placed a model that predicts how many will graduate. Well it looks amazing cause you are looking back to Harvard students (who already made it) and the only failures  are more minor ones (the ones who dropped out in between). If you go all the way back to account for thousands of applicants (winners and losers) then your model may not look as good.

Other examples would be that yeah it performs great... but all the time or when? Cause maybe it works amazing during market regime type A, but it blows up bad in other market regimes. How does this model ensure it survives or even find way to be profitable in various different regimes? 

To truly stress test it you need source code and they won't  give it to you because   
1. Company asset secret  
2. If it was that valuable they would not need to crowdfund it and share with unnecessary middlemen like the retails. Performance that stellar there are players in the industry that would pay premium.  
3. It's a con cherry picked misleading ad where the jig will be up as soon as credible third parties test it and bust the truth wide open (and/or flood of bad reviews  from retails who got smoked)

I'm not saying there is no such thing as "it's too good to be true" because they do exists but they are rare af and almost all of them don't ever advertise in public.

comments.author: agonzamart
comments.body:
I have so many thoughts on this. You cannot stress test AIs that predict the future. If you predict the future 100%, you are a magician, not real. The best you can do is look at what it predicted in the past and avoid overfitting and underfitting.

When we say the AI predicts, it can predict many different things. Is it going to go up or down? Is it going to hit this price? Is it going to be delisted or go bankrupt? All of those probably have different algorithms, models, and logic behind them. In the model, is Nvidia a number, a price, news trends, insider buys, or all of it together? So when someone says the AI predicts something, it depends a lot on *what* is predicted, *how* it's predicted, and *how* it’s used. Models can predict a future growth value and that can be your output, or that could feed another million models that use it to guide their outcomes. It’s funny to me to hear about AI like a magical box entity. It’s all about the data, the model, and the context. The exact same things a human analyst would use to make a decision. The AI can just analyze, ingest, and understand all of these better than a single human can.

I feel that the best approach is one that focuses on stacking the odds in your favor, understanding that predicting the future as a fact is impossible. But with enough information, one can infer the proper direction that allows you to make the most appropriate bet at a certain time. It’s not only about what will go up and down, it's also a game of allocating capital to maximize profits. Should I put my money here or there? Which is a problem on its own. That's why investment is such an interesting problem to look at.
